briefings.title: Amazon Inks Deal with OpenAI, Plans New AWS Applications
briefings.tldr: AWS has effectively ended Microsoft’s exclusivity over OpenAI by integrating its frontier models into the Bedrock platform while simultaneously launching "Amazon Quick," a new desktop AI productivity application, signaling a strategic push into the enterprise software layer.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
AWS has effectively ended Microsoft’s exclusivity over OpenAI by integrating its frontier models into the Bedrock platform while simultaneously launching "Amazon Quick," a new desktop AI productivity application, signaling a strategic push into the enterprise software layer.

## The OpenAI Partnership & Bedrock Integration
* **Frontier Model Access:** Moving beyond "open-weighted" models, AWS is now offering OpenAI’s frontier models (including version 5.4 in preview and 5.5 shortly) via Amazon Bedrock. 
* **Managed Agents Collaboration:** AWS and OpenAI are co-developing "Managed Agents Featuring OpenAI," a capability allowing customers to build stateful, agentic applications within the AWS security environment.
* **Infrastructure and Training:** OpenAI has made a significant commitment to using AWS infrastructure, specifically targeting AWS's proprietary **Trainium** chips to scale their business.
* **Customer Choice:** CEO Matt Garman noted that enterprise customers previously had to leave the AWS ecosystem to access OpenAI; this deal allows them to keep their data and applications centralized in AWS while using their preferred models.

## New AI-Powered Applications: Quick and Connect
* **Amazon Quick Desktop App:** AWS is launching a dedicated desktop productivity assistant designed to work across email, Slack, and local files.
    * **Contextual Learning:** The app "learns" the user’s coworkers, communication style, and workflow over time to act as a personalized productivity enhancer.
* **Amazon Connect & Enterprise Agents:** AWS is applying agentic AI to traditional enterprise sectors like healthcare, supply chain, and contact centers.
    * **Industry Expertise:** Garman aims to use Amazon’s internal logistics and operational expertise to "reimagine" 30- to 50-year-old business processes.
* **Strategic Motivation:** While AWS remains an infrastructure leader, the company is moving up the stack to provide a "full suite" of services, from chips and databases to consumer-facing applications.

## Market Dynamics and Competitive Strategy
* **Relationship with Microsoft:** Despite Microsoft benefiting financially from OpenAI licensing, Garman maintains that customers prefer AWS for its reliability and security. 
    * He compared the situation to hosting Microsoft SQL Server on AWS, noting that customers often find third-party software runs better on the AWS cloud.
* **Complementary to Partners:** Garman characterized AWS applications as "complementary" rather than competitive to partners like Salesforce, SAP, and ServiceNow. 
    * For example, "Connect Decisions" acts as an agentic helper that sits on top of existing supply chain solutions.
* **Supply Constraints:** Demand for AI capacity—specifically power, chips, and memory—continues to outstrip global supply. Garman noted that OpenAI would likely take "more capacity" than AWS can currently provide.
* **Growth Metrics:** Garman highlighted the rapid growth of Codex (OpenAI’s coding model), which doubled its user base from 2 million to 4 million in a few weeks, as evidence of the massive enterprise demand for these tools.

## Notable Quotes
> "Quick is... the single best AI productivity enhancement I've tried of anything. It allows you to work across your email, your Slack, all the information on your desktop... and it learns with you as you go." — **Matt Garman**

> "We think agents are going to totally change how work is done, how jobs are efficiently done. And we think we have some opportunities to have some unique offerings in that space that really change the game." — **Matt Garman**

> "Today the world is still largely supply-constrained when it comes to AI capacity... the OpenAI team I think would gladly take more capacity from us this year and next year and the year after that." — **Matt Garman**

briefings.title: Axiom CEO on the frontier in space commerce
briefings.tldr: Axiom Space is positioning itself as the primary successor to the International Space Station (ISS) by integrating three core business pillars—spacesuit development, private astronaut training, and modular commercial infrastructure—to meet a global demand for space access that currently exceeds available supply.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
Axiom Space is positioning itself as the primary successor to the International Space Station (ISS) by integrating three core business pillars—spacesuit development, private astronaut training, and modular commercial infrastructure—to meet a global demand for space access that currently exceeds available supply.

## Core Business Pillars & The Artemis Program
*   **Next-Generation Spacesuits:** Axiom is developing the suits for the Artemis III mission, which will return humans to the lunar surface.
    *   **Timeline:** A qualification suit will be delivered to NASA for ground testing later this year, with a flight demonstration scheduled for 2025.
    *   **Scaling Production:** NASA’s program restructuring has increased suit demand; Axiom is currently manufacturing five suits and managing a complex supply chain to support Artemis 4 and beyond.
*   **Astronaut Training:** To date, the company has flown 12 people from 11 different nations to the ISS. 
*   **Axiom Station:** The company is building a commercial replacement for the ISS, which is scheduled for retirement at the end of the decade.

## The Surge in Private Astronaut Missions (PAMs)
*   **Launch Manifest:** Historically, NASA has permitted one private mission per year. In 2025, this will double to two missions per year (Axiom will handle PAM 5; the company Vast will handle PAM 6).
*   **Supply vs. Demand:** CEO Jonathan Cirtain notes that demand from sovereign nations (such as ESA member states, Canada, and India) far exceeds current seat capacity.
*   **Democratization of Space:** Axiom provides a "Neil Armstrong moment" for emerging space nations.
    *   **Recent Partners:** Missions have recently included astronauts from Hungary, Poland, and India.
    *   **Economic Ecosystem:** These missions allow nations to develop payloads and conduct research without the overhead of building their own launch infrastructure.

## Transition to Commercial In-Orbit Infrastructure
*   **Axiom Station Timeline:**
    *   **2028:** Module 1 launches and attaches to the ISS to earn human spaceflight certification.
    *   **2029:** Module 2 launches and mates with Module 1 at 425 kilometers, creating a fully functional, four-person autonomous station.
*   **Market Opportunity:** While sovereign astronauts remain the dominant revenue source, Axiom expects significant growth in **In-Space Manufacturing** by 2032. 
    *   **Target Sectors:** Pharmaceuticals and life sciences.
    *   **Advantage:** Unlike the ISS, a commercial station has fewer barriers to entry and can prioritize experiments with the highest return on investment (ROI).

## Competitive Landscape and Capital Strategy
*   **Market Differentiators:** Cirtain argues Axiom has "no peer" because it is the only company combining a spacesuit program, a training program, and a station development program using a "derived legacy supply chain."
*   **The "SpaceX Effect":** A potential SpaceX IPO is expected to drive massive interest and liquidity into the aerospace sector, benefiting existing public players like Rocket Lab and Intuitive Machines.
*   **Axiom IPO Prospects:** Cirtain describes the business as "capital-intensive" and "equity-driven," noting that the public markets are likely the ultimate destination for Axiom to fund its long-term infrastructure goals.

***

## Notable Quotes

> "The International Space Station is set to retire at the end of the decade and we're building a commercial replacement for that space station... The next man and first woman to walk on the moon, explore the moon, will be in an Axiom suit." — **Jonathan Cirtain, CEO**

> "For the foreseeable future, the market for astronauts will be dominated by sovereign nations. But as manufacturing opportunities start to emerge, I do believe that private sector astronauts will fly to the space station to do their work—not for the thrill, but because their production... warrants that investment." — **Jonathan Cirtain, CEO**

> "Axiom's ultimate endpoint is probably in the public capital markets. It's an equity-driven business, it's a capital-intensive business, and so accessing the capital that we need to create these space stations probably is best to go out to the public markets at some point." — **Jonathan Cirtain, CEO**

briefings.title: Box CEO: Why Big Companies Are Falling Behind on AI | a16z
briefings.tldr: The gap between Silicon Valley’s AI adoption and the rest of the world is driven by a fundamental technology divide; enterprise success requires shifting from "integrating AI into software" to treating AI as an autonomous user while overcoming a massive "integration wall" that AI cannot solve on its own.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
The gap between Silicon Valley’s AI adoption and the rest of the world is driven by a fundamental technology divide; enterprise success requires shifting from "integrating AI into software" to treating AI as an autonomous user while overcoming a massive "integration wall" that AI cannot solve on its own.

## The Silicon Valley vs. Enterprise Divide
*   **Technical Aptitude Gap:** Silicon Valley workflows benefit from high technical aptitude where users debug their own tools. In contrast, enterprise knowledge work is characterized by less technical users and highly fragmented legacy systems.
*   **Diffusion Speed:** AI agents work effectively in startup environments because work is verifiable (e.g., code). In broader knowledge work, diffusion will take years as organizations grapple with "masses of stuff" that require manual integration.
*   **Decision-Making Styles:**
    *   **Startups:** Adoption starts with individuals making agile, local choices.
    *   **Enterprises:** Decisions are made centrally through boards and CEOs, often leading to top-down mandates that lack operational alignment.

## Why Enterprise AI Initiatives Fail
*   **The 95% Failure Rate:** Reports (such as from MIT) suggest the vast majority of enterprise AI efforts fail. This is often due to "consultant-led" centralized projects that don't understand how the actual work happens on the ground.
*   **Incentive Misalignment:** Some large companies are mistakenly incentivizing AI use by measuring token counts.
    *   **Fake Productivity:** Employees are reportedly tasking agents with useless work simply to meet usage metrics, creating "problematic artifacts" and technical noise.
*   **Architectural Paralysis:** The rapid pace of AI innovation (labs "leapfrogging" each other) creates nervousness among CIOs. Architecture teams are afraid to "get in bed" with a specific paradigm that may be deprecated within months.

## The Architectural Shift: AI as a User
*   **Moving Beyond Chat:** Early AI integration focused on adding "chat" features into existing products. The panel argues this hybrid model is largely failing.
*   **The "Headless" SaaS Model:** A significant mental shift is occurring where software is treated as a CLI (Command Line Interface) tool and AI is treated as the user.
    *   **Product Evolution:** Companies are being forced to re-architect software twice in a year—first to add AI features, then to make the software consumable by autonomous agents.
*   **Search vs. Action:** AI's first major value add in the enterprise is "seeking and presenting" information across fragmented files. The "acting" phase (agents that do work) will require significantly more infrastructure modernization.

## The Integration Wall
*   **Security and Access Controls:** Agents cannot "ask Sally" for access to a restricted file. Most legacy environments lack authoritative access controls, meaning agents hit immediate "walls" that humans bypass through social networking.
*   **The Manual Labor of Automation:** There is a paradox where "automating people" requires hiring thousands of people.
    *   **System Integrators:** The need for firms like Accenture and Deloitte is growing because change management and system implementation remain the primary bottlenecks.
*   **Data Fragmentation:** AI does not fix "dirty" or disconnected data. Any enterprise older than ten years is essentially a mass of unintegrated systems that AI cannot magically stitch together without human intervention.

## Technical Entropy and the Future of Jobs
*   **The Complexity Trap:** The belief that AI code generation will eliminate the need for engineers is a fallacy.
    *   **Entropy:** More AI-generated code leads to more complex systems, which increases the demand for human engineers to handle system upgrades, downtime, and security incidents.
*   **Job Creation vs. Destruction:** While AI automates specific tasks, it creates new categories of work in maintenance and integration.
    *   **Dead Web Comparison:** Just as the internet led to thousands of "dead" internal team websites, AI runs the risk of creating "useless artifacts" that require human oversight to prune and manage.

## Notable Quotes

> "The thing that's not different about AI—that agents don't fix—is that any enterprise of a thousand people or more, older than ten years, is just a mass of stuff sitting there waiting to be integrated. AI actually doesn't help to integrate anything." — **Steven Sinofsky**

> "Instead of viewing AI as software, view it as a user. Take your product, make it a CLI tool, and then have the AI be an agent that actually uses it. This is a very significant architectural and mental shift." — **Martin Casado**

> "People thought it was somewhat ironic that we need people to implement the agents that are going to go automate the people. No, that's exactly how it works. You need lots and lots of work to be in a position where agents can actually help you." — **Aaron Levie**

briefings.title: LIVE: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda Press Conference After Policy Meeting in Tokyo | AF1Z
briefings.tldr: The Bank of Japan (BoJ) has signaled its intention to continue raising interest rates as inflation is projected to remain aligned with its 2% target through FY2028, despite significant economic risks posed by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
The Bank of Japan (BoJ) has signaled its intention to continue raising interest rates as inflation is projected to remain aligned with its 2% target through FY2028, despite significant economic risks posed by geopolitical tensions in the Middle East.

## Economic and Inflation Outlook (FY2026–2028)
* **Price Projections:** Governor Kazuo Ueda noted that inflation (excluding fresh food) is expected to stay in the upper 2% range for FY2026, settling toward 2% in FY2027 and FY2028.
    * **Upward Revision:** The price outlook for FY2026 was revised significantly upward compared to the previous report.
    * **Wage-Price Cycle:** The mechanism where wage increases lead to price hikes remains intact, and medium- to long-term inflation expectations are rising.
* **GDP Growth:** Japan’s economy is expected to continue a moderate recovery.
    * **Short-term Headwinds:** Growth may slow in FY2026 as high oil prices weigh on corporate profits and household real income.
    * **Long-term Recovery:** Recovery is expected to accelerate again from FY2027 as the negative impact of high energy prices fades and the cycle of income-to-spending strengthens.

## Geopolitical Risks and Oil Price Assumptions
* **Middle East Uncertainty:** The BoJ’s core outlook assumes that Middle East tensions will ease and large-scale supply chain disruptions will be avoided.
    * **Oil Pricing:** The forecast is based on Dubai crude starting at approximately $105 per barrel and gradually declining to the $70 range by the end of the forecast period.
* **Dual Risk Profile:** Ueda highlighted a divergent risk balance for FY2026:
    * **Economic Downside:** Prolonged tensions and high oil prices pose a significant downside risk to economic growth.
    * **Inflation Upside:** Conversely, these same factors pose an upside risk to prices, as oil serves as a primary raw material across various industries.

## Monetary Policy Stance
* **Interest Rate Path:** Ueda stated that because real interest rates are currently "extremely low," the BoJ will continue to raise the policy rate if economic and price developments align with their projections.
* **Policy Normalization:** The BoJ aims to adjust the degree of monetary easing to ensure the sustainable and stable achievement of the 2% price target.
    * **Timing and Pace:** Future adjustments will be determined by monitoring the Middle East situation and the degree of certainty regarding the central price outlook.
* **Internal Governance:** The board rejected proposals from members Takata and Tamura to describe price stability as "already achieved" or "closely aligned," opting for a more cautious official description of the progress.

## Shifting Corporate Behavior
* **Price-Setting Activity:** Ueda observed that Japanese companies are becoming more proactive in adjusting wages and prices compared to historical trends.
* **Impact of Cost Shocks:** Due to this shift, increases in raw material costs (like oil) are now passing through to a wider range of goods and services more easily than in the past, potentially accelerating underlying inflation.

***

**Notable Quotes**

> "Given that current real interest rates are at an extremely low level, we will continue to raise the policy rate and adjust the degree of monetary easing in accordance with the economic, price, and financial situation." — **Kazuo Ueda, BoJ Governor**

> "Specifically regarding prices, we must be sufficiently mindful of the risk that inflation could significantly overshoot, which could subsequently have a negative impact on the economy." — **Kazuo Ueda, BoJ Governor**

> "Middle East developments could significantly change our economic and price outlook; we believe it is necessary to monitor these impacts on financial and foreign exchange markets very closely." — **Kazuo Ueda, BoJ Governor**

briefings.title: Lessons From a Life in the Markets | Paul Tudor Jones Interview
briefings.tldr: Legendary trader Paul Tudor Jones reflects on a 50-year career defined by "fighting in the trenches" of macro markets, contrasts his high-volatility trading style with the "genius" of Warren Buffett’s compounding, and issues urgent warnings regarding a global sovereign debt bubble and the unregulated existential risks of AI.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Legendary trader Paul Tudor Jones reflects on a 50-year career defined by "fighting in the trenches" of macro markets, contrasts his high-volatility trading style with the "genius" of Warren Buffett’s compounding, and issues urgent warnings regarding a global sovereign debt bubble and the unregulated existential risks of AI.

## Trading Philosophy and the Macro Outlook
*   **The Power of Trend Following:** Paul Tudor Jones (PTJ) asserts that the most significant wealth is created by riding a single trend for the longest possible time.
*   **Trading vs. Investing:** PTJ describes his career as a "Right Guard in the NFL," constantly fighting for alpha in the trenches, whereas investors like Warren Buffett succeed through a "belief system" in long-term growth and the power of compound interest. 
    *   **Alpha Correlation:** PTJ’s BVI fund maintains a -0.12 correlation with the S&P 500, meaning 100% of its returns are pure alpha rather than market beta.
*   **Liquidity Lessons:** A formative experience was the 1980 silver collapse. Witnessing Bunker Hunt go from the world’s richest man to nearly bankrupt in six weeks instilled a permanent respect for liquidity.
*   **Current Market Warning:** PTJ warns of a "sovereign debt bubble" and extreme over-equitization.
    *   **Valuation Extremes:** US stock market cap to GDP is currently 252%, compared to 65% in 1929 and 170% in 2000. 
    *   **Reverse Wealth Effect:** A mean reversion to historical P/E ratios could trigger a 35% market decline, potentially wiping out capital gains tax revenue and exploding the budget deficit.
*   **Bitcoin and Gold:** PTJ views Bitcoin as the "ultimate inflation hedge" due to its finite supply, though he acknowledges risks from cyber warfare and quantum computing.

## The Existential Risks of AI
*   **The Safety Gap:** PTJ expresses deep alarm over the "build-break-iterate" model of AI development. Unlike previous technologies, a "break" in AI could result in a tail event involving millions of deaths.
*   **Regulatory Failure:** He compares the current lack of AI regulation to the post-WWII era, where Congress quickly created the Atomic Energy Commission to manage nuclear risks. He advocates for immediate federal and international regulation.
*   **The Watermarking Mandate:** To restore social trust, PTJ proposes that all AI-generated content must be watermarked, suggesting that knowingly violating this requirement should be a felony.
*   **Social Disruption:** PTJ fears AI will replace so many jobs that humans will struggle to find "significance," which historically has been tied to work.

## Discipline, Routine, and Execution
*   **A "Day in the Life":** PTJ maintains a rigorous schedule:
    *   **Early Starts:** Wakes at 6:15 AM; often wakes at 2:30 or 3:00 AM to watch the London market open and perform analytical work.
    *   **Information Management:** Processes 800 to 1,000 emails daily. He notes that today's information overload makes "exquisite execution" (buying at maximum fear, selling at maximum elation) harder than it was in the 1980s.
*   **Journalism as a Business Tool:** PTJ believes "Journalism 101" is more valuable than a business degree. It teaches "Principal Component Analysis"—putting the most important information first (the "Who, What, Where, When, Why") and communicating concisely in 15 seconds or less.
*   **Longevity Philosophy:** PTJ stays active to keep his mind sharp, citing an 83-year-old doctor's advice: "You retire, you die."

## Philanthropy and Finding Significance
*   **The Robin Hood Foundation:** Founded by PTJ in 1988, the organization applies rigorous business metrics to poverty-fighting. He credits the foundation's success to the financial community's desire to find "significance" through service.
*   **The Multiplicative Power of Kindness:** PTJ shares a story from age three when an elderly Black man helped him find his mother in a market. That single act of kindness led to decades of daily prayers, which eventually inspired PTJ’s massive philanthropic efforts in Bed-Stuy and beyond.
*   **Redefining Legacy:** PTJ views his professional success merely as a tool to facilitate meaningful deeds. He defines a great life through the "Principal Components" of God, family, friends, and service.

***

> "Warren [Buffett], if you happen to hear this, I'm deeply apologetic. You are the OG of compound interest and I wish I was one-tenth as smart as you are." — **Paul Tudor Jones**

> "Better than a business school degree is Journalism 101... It teaches you to write where the conclusion comes first... putting the most important stuff at the beginning." — **Paul Tudor Jones**

> "The point here is that one simple act of kindness can have waves of betterment. It can be so transformative and so multiplicative." — **Paul Tudor Jones**

> "You're only worth what you can write a check for tomorrow." — **Paul Tudor Jones** (quoting his grandfather)

briefings.title: T-Mobile Q1 2026 Earnings Call Livestream
briefings.tldr: T-Mobile delivered a strong Q1 2026 performance, raising full-year guidance for EBITDA and free cash flow while emphasizing a "widening differentiation" strategy that leverages network superiority to drive industry-leading growth in mobile, broadband, and emerging AI sectors.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
T-Mobile delivered a strong Q1 2026 performance, raising full-year guidance for EBITDA and free cash flow while emphasizing a "widening differentiation" strategy that leverages network superiority to drive industry-leading growth in mobile, broadband, and emerging AI sectors.

## Financial Performance and Guidance Raise
* **Updated 2026 Guidance:** On the strength of Q1 momentum, leadership raised several full-year targets:
    * **Core Adjusted EBITDA:** Now expected to be between $37.1 billion and $37.5 billion.
    * **Adjusted Free Cash Flow:** Raised to between $18.1 billion and $18.7 billion.
    * **Postpaid Net Account Additions:** Increased to a range of 950,000 to 1,050,000.
* **Service Revenue Growth:** Postpaid service revenue grew 15% year-over-year, with total service revenue up 11%—a rate CFO Peter Osvaldik noted is more than four times that of the nearest competitor.
* **ARPA Expansion:** Postpaid Average Revenue Per Account (ARPA) grew 3.9% in Q1.
    * **Premium Mix:** Over 60% of new accounts are selecting premium-tier rate plans.
* **Capital Allocation:** The company increased its 2026 stockholder return authorization by $3.6 billion, bringing the total authorization to $18.2 billion.

## Broadband and Fiber Expansion
* **Market Leadership:** T-Mobile remains the fastest-growing ISP in America, adding over 500,000 total broadband customers in Q1.
* **New Fiber Joint Ventures:** CEO Srini Gopalan announced two new JVs with infrastructure partners to acquire **GoNetSpeed, Greenlight Networks, and i3 Broadband**.
    * **Strategic Focus:** The company is prioritizing "first to fiber" assets and local scale over a specific "homes passed" target to ensure double-digit IRRs.
    * **Integration:** T-Mobile will manage all retail consumer operations for these assets, using a common IT platform to ensure a unified customer experience.
* **Business Super Broadband:** In partnership with SpaceX/Starlink, T-Mobile is launching a "Super Broadband" product for B2B customers, providing satellite-based redundancy and nationwide coverage for businesses.

## Network Innovation and Physical AI
* **5G Advanced and Robotics:** T-Mobile is connecting its 5G Advanced network to **Figure AI’s F3 humanoid robots**.
    * **Edge Inferencing:** CTO Dr. John Saw highlighted that the network's low latency and "fallow compute" capabilities at the edge are being designed specifically to support the evolution of physical AI.
* **Network-Native AI:** The company is beta-testing a "live translation" application that translates voices into 80 languages directly through the network core, requiring no third-party apps.
* **Business Applications:** The "automated ball-strike system" recently rolled out by Major League Baseball (MLB) was cited as a primary example of 5G Advanced being used for real-time challenge systems.

## Market Differentiation and Governance
* **Customer Loyalty:** T-Mobile reported an industry-leading Net Promoter Score (NPS) of 45, which is 20% higher than its closest competitor.
* **Postpaid Account Churn:** Leadership addressed a slight rise in account churn, attributing it to the mathematical weighting of the high-growth broadband business, which structurally has higher churn than wireless.
* **Merger Speculation:** Addressing rumors regarding a merger with Deutsche Telekom, Srini Gopalan clarified that such a transaction would require a "majority of the minority" approval process by disinterested shareholders.
* **Rural and Business Growth:** T-Mobile currently holds only a 24% share in smaller markets and rural areas, representing what Gopalan called a "substantial growth runway" as network perception improves.

> "Our strategy is driven by widening differentiation, providing customers with the best network, best value, and best experience, all in the same place so that they don't need to make trade-offs anymore." — **Srini Gopalan, President and CEO**

> "We see our strength as attacking incumbents rather than becoming an incumbent. We see a huge opportunity to attack incumbents across fiber and FWA; that'll be our key play." — **Srini Gopalan, President and CEO**

> "It’s our product. It’s what we sell to customers. And the differentiation that we’re starting to see with consumer sentiment now following what the actual network progress is... means that it’s not just devices that make customers come here." — **Peter Osvaldik, CFO**

> "We didn't build a 5G advanced network just for faster phones; we actually built it for physical AI... we believe that we have a multi-year advantage over the competition for this." — **Dr. John Saw, CTO**

briefings.title: The Iran oil shock: will it force the world to re-think the future of energy?
briefings.tldr: The 2026 oil shock, triggered by the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, represents the largest energy supply disruption in history, forcing a global shift away from energy interdependence toward domestic "autarky" and accelerated electrification.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
The 2026 oil shock, triggered by the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, represents the largest energy supply disruption in history, forcing a global shift away from energy interdependence toward domestic "autarky" and accelerated electrification.

## The Magnitude of the 2026 Oil Shock
*   **Historic Supply Disruption:** Somewhere between 13 to 15 million barrels of oil per day—approximately 10% to 15% of global supply—are currently offline due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
    *   This disruption is significantly larger than the 1973 Arab oil embargo (7%) or the Gulf War (6%).
*   **Infrastructure Vulnerability:** While physical infrastructure damage has been limited so far (mostly affecting Qatari natural gas), a resolution is not immediate. 
    *   **Recovery Timeline:** Even if the Strait opened today, it would take weeks to months to restore supply due to production "shut-ins" and maritime insurance/safety concerns.
    *   **The Insurance Premium:** Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which bypasses the Strait, serves as a primary example of "energy insurance" that countries will now be more willing to pay for.
*   **Regional Disparity:** The shock is hitting emerging markets in Southeast Asia and lower-income nations like Bangladesh and Pakistan hardest, causing physical fuel shortages and school closures. The U.S. remains somewhat more insulated due to its high domestic production levels.

## The Allure of "Energy Autarky"
*   **Strategic Liability:** Historically, energy security was built on interconnection and global trade. In the current fragmented geopolitical landscape, countries now view integration as a risk rather than a source of resilience.
*   **The Impulse for Self-Sufficiency:** Nations are trending toward "autarky"—the desire to produce all energy within their own borders to avoid Middle Eastern geopolitical turmoil.
    *   **Economic Cost:** Trade generally lowers costs; moving toward a "fortress approach" is significantly more expensive and requires massive investment in redundant infrastructure.
*   **Swapping Dependencies:** Transitioning to domestic clean energy reduces oil dependence but creates new vulnerabilities.
    *   **China’s Dominance:** Approximately 70% to 90% of the supply chain for clean energy (batteries, solar panels, and critical minerals) is controlled by China.

## National Security as a Catalyst for Energy Transition
*   **The Situation Room Effect:** Jason Bordoff notes that national security concerns often motivate government action more effectively than climate change warnings. The current crisis may drive a faster transition than environmental policy alone.
*   **Electrification vs. Addition:** Bordoff clarifies that the world has historically engaged in "energy addition" (adding renewables while still increasing fossil fuel use) rather than a true "transition."
    *   **Displacement:** For a real transition to occur, clean energy must grow fast enough to displace the 80% of the energy mix currently held by fossil fuels—a figure that has remained stagnant for decades.
*   **Emerging Market Shifts:** High oil prices are driving a surge in electric vehicle (EV) adoption in developing nations; for example, Chinese automaker BYD is seeing record sales in Brazil and the Philippines as consumers flee high pump prices.

## Long-Term Structural Challenges
*   **Short-Termism in Policy:** Politicians often react to oil shocks with temporary fixes (releasing strategic reserves or waiving taxes) rather than long-term structural changes. 
    *   **The Urgency Gap:** Once the immediate crisis fades, the political will to fund expensive energy insurance typically evaporates.
*   **AI and Data Centers:** The "age of electrification" is being strained by the energy requirements of AI and data centers. 
    *   **Investment Risk:** Regions like the UAE and Saudi Arabia were positioning themselves as hubs for data centers, but the current conflict may alter the "risk profile" for tech firms looking to place physical infrastructure in the Gulf.
*   **The Hard-to-Abate Sectors:** While cars are easily electrified, Bordoff warns that steel and cement production—which account for double the emissions of all the world’s cars combined—require "molecules" rather than just "electrons," making them harder to secure during an oil and gas shock.

## Notable Quotes

> "This is the largest oil supply disruption the world has ever seen... there’s no policy tool in the policy toolkit large enough to deal with a shock that large." — **Jason Bordoff**

> "In a world of fragmentation [and] geopolitical conflict... countries don’t view interconnection as security; they view it as a risk. And it’s going to lead to an impulse, an allure of autarky." — **Jason Bordoff**

> "The most durable thing you can do for energy security is just to use less in the first place." — **Jason Bordoff**

> "Most of the things you would want to do to deal with an oil shock don’t help with this oil shock; they help with the next oil shock." — **Jason Bordoff**

briefings.title: Tim Cook’s Impeccable Timing | Stratechery by Ben Thompson
briefings.tldr: Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure as Apple CEO transitioned the company from a "zero-to-one" innovator under Steve Jobs to a "1-to-n" operational juggernaut, increasing Apple's valuation from $297 billion to $4 trillion while leaving behind critical long-term questions regarding AI and China.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure as Apple CEO transitioned the company from a "zero-to-one" innovator under Steve Jobs to a "1-to-n" operational juggernaut, increasing Apple's valuation from $297 billion to $4 trillion while leaving behind critical long-term questions regarding AI and China.

## The Financial and Operational Legacy
* **Staggering Growth Metrics:** Under Cook’s leadership (2011–2026), Apple’s revenue increased by 303%, profits by 354%, and its market value grew by a massive 1,251%.
* **Operational Genius:** Cook transformed Apple from a company with its own struggling factories into a global supply chain powerhouse. 
    * **Just-in-Time Supply:** He shifted the manufacturing base to China, creating a worldwide network capable of delivering hundreds of millions of units across expanded product lines (e.g., five iPhone models instead of one).
    * **Product Reliability:** Despite the massive scale, Cook’s tenure was marked by a lack of significant product recalls or major operational failures.
* **1-to-n Execution:** While Steve Jobs focused on "vertical progress" (creating new categories like the iPhone and iPad), Cook focused on "horizontal progress," perfecting and expanding those categories to their maximum financial potential.

## The Cook Doctrine and Services Pivot
* **The "Cook Doctrine":** Originating from Apple University, this philosophy emphasizes owning primary technologies, focusing on a few meaningful projects, and maintaining the "self-honesty" to change course when wrong.
* **The Services Engine:** Cook elevated Services (App Store, iCloud, Google Search deal) into a primary financial pillar.
    * **Profitability:** Services now account for 26% of revenue and a disproportionate 41% of total profit.
    * **Developer Friction:** Critics like John Gruber argue Cook prioritized Apple’s bottom line over the health of the developer ecosystem, potentially damaging long-term platform loyalty.
* **Wearables Success:** While products like Apple Watch and AirPods are derivative of the iPhone, they became a $35.4 billion business, equivalent to a top-150 Fortune 500 company.

## Strategic Risks: China and AI
* **The China Violation:** In a reversal of the "Cook Doctrine" (which advocates for owning and controlling destiny), Cook made Apple almost entirely dependent on China for manufacturing and increasingly for industrial design.
    * **Geopolitical Vulnerability:** This dependence leaves Apple uniquely exposed to deteriorating U.S.-China relations.
* **The AI Dilemma:** Apple has avoided the massive infrastructure spending of its peers, opting instead to white-label Google’s technology for the "new Siri."
    * **Short-term vs. Long-term:** While financially prudent now, this decision risks ceding the future of integrated AI to competitors who own the underlying models and infrastructure.

## Succession and Future Outlook
* **John Ternus Takes the Reins:** Cook is stepping down as CEO to become Executive Chairman, handing the role to John Ternus at a time when the iPhone and Mac (boosted by Apple Silicon) are at record performance levels.
* **Impeccable Timing:** Cook departs following Apple’s best-ever quarter, securing his legacy as a financial titan. 
* **The Looming "Crash Out":** The briefing suggests that while Cook maximized the Jobs era, the next CEO must determine if Apple can still innovate "zero-to-one" or if it has become permanently dependent on third parties for the next era of computing.

> "We believe that we’re on the face of the Earth to make great products, and that’s not changing. We’re constantly focusing on innovating. We believe in the simple, not the complex. We believe that we need to own and control the primary technologies behind the products we make." — **Tim Cook**

> "Jobs might have been responsible for taking Apple to zero to one, but it was Cook that took Apple from $1 to $436 billion in revenue and $118 billion in profit last year. It’s a testimony to his capabilities and execution that Apple didn’t suffer any sort of post-founder hangover." — **Ben Thompson**

> "Tim Cook built what is arguably Apple’s most important technology, its ability to build the world’s best personal computer products at astronomical scale, and did so in a way that leaves Apple more vulnerable than anyone to the deteriorating relationship between the United States and China." — **Ben Thompson**

briefings.title: What happens now that AI is good at math? — the OpenAI Podcast Ep. 17
briefings.tldr: OpenAI researchers Sébastien Bubeck and Ernest Ryu detail how AI has evolved from basic arithmetic to solving 40-year-old open mathematical problems, signaling a shift toward "automated researchers" that can reason over weeks or months—a critical milestone for AGI.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
OpenAI researchers Sébastien Bubeck and Ernest Ryu detail how AI has evolved from basic arithmetic to solving 40-year-old open mathematical problems, signaling a shift toward "automated researchers" that can reason over weeks or months—a critical milestone for AGI.

## The Rapid Ascent of AI Math Capabilities
* **From Basic Logic to Research-Level:** Just two years ago, AI lacked formal reasoning models. Today, models have achieved gold-medal performance on International Math Olympiad (IMO) problems and are assisting Fields Medalists in their daily research.
* **Solving 42-Year-Old Problems:** Ernest Ryu used ChatGPT to resolve a 42-year-old open problem regarding the Nesterov accelerated gradient method. 
    * **Efficiency Gains:** Ryu completed the proof in 12 hours of interaction with the model—a task he estimated would have taken over 40 hours of manual effort with a high risk of failure.
* **The Erdős Problem Milestone:** OpenAI models have recently generated solutions to 10+ Erdős problems (longstanding challenges in combinatorics).
    * **Original Discovery:** While early successes involved "deep literature searches" (connecting existing but disparate research), recent outputs include original, publishable discoveries not found in current literature.

## Why Mathematics is the Foundation for AGI
* **The Ultimate Benchmark:** Math is the perfect training ground for AI because the questions are non-ambiguous and the answers are objectively verifiable.
* **Zero-Tolerance Reasoning:** Unlike creative writing, a mathematical proof fails if a single link in a 50-page chain of logic is flawed. This forces models to develop "consistency" and "self-correction," traits essential for general intelligence.
* **Scaling "AGI Time":** Researchers are moving beyond "AGI seconds" (brief tasks) to "AGI days and weeks." 
    * **Long-Horizon Autonomy:** The goal is an "automated researcher" that can work autonomously over long timelines, summarizing ideas into notes and iterating on them over months, much like a human mathematician.

## Impact on Global Scientific Research
* **Generalization Across Fields:** The reasoning techniques developed for math are being applied to biology, chemistry, and material science.
* **The End of Niche Silos:** AI acts as a "connective tissue" for science. It can read hyper-niche papers from decades ago and surface relevant connections to modern problems that a human specialist would likely miss.
* **Verification and Trust:** AI has the "patience" to verify 300-page proofs that are often too grueling for human peer reviewers, helping to purge the literature of "fatal mistakes" and minor errors.
* **Democratizing Expertise:** Advanced mathematical tools allow non-mathematicians (like physicists or chemists) to utilize complex differential geometry or optimization theory without needing a PhD-level grasp of those specific sub-fields.

## The Evolving Role of Humans
* **The Danger of Mental Atrophy:** Bubeck warns against "handing the keys to the castle" to AI. If humans stop doing the "hard work" of deep thinking, they will lose the expertise required to verify AI outputs.
* **Human as Director:** The role of the scientist is shifting from "calculator" to "visionary." While AI can solve problems and even ask new questions, humans must provide the "understanding" and prioritize which problems—such as curing diseases—actually matter to society.
* **A Call for More Scientists:** Contrary to fears of displacement, the researchers argue we need *more* scientists than ever. These tools will allow scientists to be more productive and move the "frontier of knowledge" faster than previously possible.

## Notable Quotes

> "The progress of the last few years has been nothing short of miraculous. It's important to remember that two years ago, we didn't even have reasoning models... Today, the models are able to help Fields Medalists in their day-to-day work." 
— **Sébastien Bubeck**

> "A mathematical proof... if at some point in your chain of reasoning there is a mistake, this will kill the entire argument. This property makes it what you want out of reasoning models—that if they make mistakes, they will be able to correct themselves." 
— **Sébastien Bubeck**

> "We will be able to have LLMs be able to solve problems that require more than 50 pages of thinking. And that's what humans do... over several months we've thought for so long, but it's summarized and organized in a way that becomes manageable." 
— **Ernest Ryu**

> "I'm worried about potentially having a shallower understanding of things because we rely too much on the tool. Expertise is even more valuable than it ever was... If it wasn't for that deep understanding, we would not be able to push the state of the art." 
— **Sébastien Bubeck**

briefings.title: What's a winning culture | Investment Conference 2025 | Norges Bank Investment Management

people.name: Jamie Dimon
people.role: Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, JP Morgan Chase

people.name: Kenneth C. Griffin
people.role: Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Citadel

briefings.tldr: While strategy and technology can be easily replicated, corporate culture is the ultimate, non-copyable competitive advantage that determines long-term survival.
briefings.summary_markdown:
## TL;DR
While strategy and technology can be easily replicated, corporate culture is the ultimate, non-copyable competitive advantage that determines long-term survival. As organizations navigate the disruptive rise of AI and generational leadership transitions, winning companies are defined by high-agency decision-making, extreme execution, and the alignment of human talent.

## Redefining "Winning" and the Core of Corporate Culture

*   **Culture as a Forward-Looking Indicator:** Nicolai Tangen (CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management) emphasized that while financial balance sheets and quarterly numbers show where a company has been, its culture is the only true indicator of where it is going. 
    *   **The Nokia Cautionary Tale:** Nokia controlled half the global mobile market in 2007, but mid-managers failed to warn executives about the threat of the newly launched iPhone due to a rigid culture of fear, leading to the company’s swift demise.
*   **The Scale of Ambition and Aspiration:** Tangen noted that "kick-ass" companies possess world-leading ambitions. Kenneth C. Griffin (Founder & CEO of Citadel) prefers the term "aspiration" over "ambition," arguing that leaders must seek out what people want to build and change rather than a specific monetary payout.
*   **Decoupling Survival from Founders:** David M. Rubenstein (Co-Founder of Carlyle) noted that very few great companies survive the demise of their founders. 
    *   **The Apple Model:** Under Tim Cook, Apple expanded on the DNA Steve Jobs built, scaling its market capitalization from $350 billion at Jobs' death to $3.5 trillion by putting customers and employees first.
*   **No "Participation Trophies":** At Citadel, winning is explicitly listed as a core value. Griffin recruits people who competed in high-level arenas (like sports or debate) because they understand how to win, lose, and maintain the mental fortitude to return to work.
    *   **The Humbling Nature of Markets:** Griffin pointed out that Citadel's average equity portfolio manager is only correct about 53% of the time, making resilience a vital life skill.
*   **Radical Cost Obsession over "Culture Smulture":** Michael O'Leary (Group CEO of Ryanair) rejected traditional corporate culture talk in favor of radical simplicity and cost obsession. 
    *   **Efficiency Drives Growth:** Ryanair has grown to Europe's largest airline by stripping out complexity (e.g., bypassing travel agents, charging for bags to reduce ground-handling labor, and operating a flat management structure with only three layers between the front line and the CEO).

## Driving Structural and Cultural Transformation

*   **Solving Execution Problems:** Karin Rådström (CEO of Daimler Truck) realized her 130-year-old engineering company did not have a strategy problem, but rather an execution problem. She introduced a "simpler, faster, stronger" mindset to dismantle rigid German corporate structures.
    *   **Dismantling Corporate Bureaucracy:** Daimler Truck systematically targets and replaces three to four bureaucratic processes every month. Rådström has reduced default PowerPoint presentations, removed non-contributing executives from meetings, and is actively shortening the traditional annual budgeting process.
*   **"Front Weeks" and Staying Grounded:** Jesper Brodin (Former CEO of Ingka Group/IKEA) stressed that leaders must actively live their culture. Through IKEA’s "front weeks"—where executives work on the retail floor—Brodin realized the company had stopped listening to customers, which catalyzed their massive, late-stage digital transformation.
    *   **Climate-Smart Cost Reductions:** By analyzing IKEA’s carbon footprint, Brodin discovered that raw materials account for 36% of its costs and are its greatest carbon footprint. Over his tenure, IKEA achieved 24% revenue growth while cutting carbon emissions by 30% through circular material innovations.
*   **Strategy and Culture as Parallel Tracks:** James P. Gorman (Chairman Emeritus of Morgan Stanley & Chairman of Disney) noted that "strategy earns you the right to talk about culture." Leaders must first establish a viable business model that gives people a promise for the future before building cultural values.
*   **Landlords vs. Tenants:** Gorman motivated Wall Street bankers by encouraging them to stop acting like "tenants looking for their next bonus" and start acting like "landlords" invested in the long-term equity value of the institution.
*   **Converting Legacy Sports Platform to Entertainment:** Stefano Domenicali (President & CEO of Formula One) transitioned F1 from a traditional motorsport into a massive global entertainment platform. By embracing social media and launching the Netflix series *Drive to Survive*, F1 captured younger, non-traditional audiences and built events that generate greater business opportunities than the Super Bowl.

## Managing Successions and Leadership Transitions

*   **Clarity, Transparency, and Intentionality:** James P. Gorman successfully managed highly complex leadership handovers at both Morgan Stanley and Disney by implementing rigorous rules:
    *   **The "No-Paper" Strategy Test:** To prevent candidates from relying on consultants, Gorman had CEO contenders write strategy papers and then subjected them to intensive, paperless Q&A sessions.
    *   **The "Absolute Exit" Rule:** Gorman asserted that "the king has to be dead for the new king to succeed." Outgoing CEOs must completely exit the operational space to prevent lingering influence or confusion.
    *   **Treating Non-Selected Candidates with Respect:** Through transparency, Gorman successfully retained the non-selected internal CEO candidates at both Morgan Stanley and Disney.
*   **The Founder-to-Professional Pivot:** Nandan Nilekani (Co-Founder and Chairman of Infosys) highlighted that transitioning leadership from a founder to a professional CEO is incredibly complex. Professional successions require an intentional re-anchoring of values so the culture survives the exit of the company's creators.

## Navigating Corporate Culture in the Age of AI

*   **Avoiding AI-Accelerated Dysfunction:** Nilekani warned that deploying AI in a politically fractured or siloed company only accelerates its organizational problems. He noted that "AI is not just applied artificial intelligence; it's aligned individuals" marching to a single drummer.
*   **Bleeding Edge vs. Leading Edge:** Good companies must choose where to be on the "bleeding edge" and where to be a fast follower.
    *   **Citadel's Approach:** When Google released the TensorFlow machine learning toolkit, Citadel developers put it into production to quote US equities within four weeks. Conversely, Griffin later killed 195 out of 200 generative AI projects at Citadel to prevent expensive ad-hoc distractions, focusing strictly on five high-impact initiatives.
*   **Shifting From Process to Calculated Risk:** Christel Heydemann (CEO of Orange Group) faces the challenge of instilling speed into a zero-risk, critical infrastructure telecom utility with 130,000 employees. She is transforming the legacy "incumbent" culture by introducing "beta testing" environments where it is safe to fail, and encouraging employees to speak up about operational failures.
*   **AI Fluency as a Cultural Decision:** Daniela Amodei (Co-Founder & President of Anthropic) explained that building AI fluency across an enterprise is a cultural decision rather than a technological one. She shared that Anthropic champions "holding light and shade"—being brutally honest about both the economic opportunities and risks of AI, even when it means delaying product launches for safety.
*   **The Emerging Market Divide and Geopolitics:** Ajay Banga (President of the World Bank) and Nilekani cautioned that the global AI narrative is currently broken because emerging markets lack the critical infrastructure—computing power, electricity, data, and skilled labor—to run Large Language Models. They predict that data will soon be treated as a critical national security asset, leading to complex geopolitical data sovereignty policies.

## Notable Quotes

> "Numbers, they tell you where a company has been. Culture tells you where it's going." 
> — **Nicolai Tangen**

> "The most junior person who is closest to the information, that's the person who optimally should make the decision as often or as frequently as possible." 
> — **Kenneth C. Griffin**

> "We're going to be good at managing problems, but we will lead from opportunities. Because that's how the world is created." 
> — **Jesper Brodin**

> "The king has to be dead for the new king to succeed." 
> — **James P. Gorman**

briefings.title: iRocket CEO Asad Malik and Sec. Wilbur Ross on the future of aerospace, drone warfare and espionage

people.name: Wilbur Ross
people.role: Former Commerce Secretary and iRocket investor

briefings.tldr: iRocket is leveraging a fully robotic, AI-driven factory to revolutionize aerospace manufacturing, significantly reducing the "cost to kill" for counter-drone systems and working toward 100% reusable launch vehicles capable of 24-hour mission turnarounds.
briefings.summary_markdown:
**TL;DR**
iRocket is leveraging a fully robotic, AI-driven factory to revolutionize aerospace manufacturing, significantly reducing the "cost to kill" for counter-drone systems and working toward 100% reusable launch vehicles capable of 24-hour mission turnarounds.

## Advanced Robotic Manufacturing and Scaling
*   **The Robotic Factory:** iRocket operates a nearly human-free production facility that utilizes a "digital twin" architecture and AI to reduce engineering overhead by 30%.
    *   **Current Output:** The facility can produce 37 Hydra missile systems per day and approximately 3,000 solid rocket motors annually.
    *   **Rapid Scaling:** CEO Asad Malik noted that the company moved from a design decision to full flight and horizontal testing in just eight weeks.
*   **Economic Advantage:** The company focuses on the "cost to kill," addressing the current economic imbalance where the U.S. might use a $4 million Patriot missile to intercept a $25,000 drone.
*   **Major Contracts:** iRocket has secured a $33 million contract with the U.S. Army for Hydra 70 missiles, which has the potential to scale to $150 million, targeting production of up to 15,000 units over the next few years.

## Shifting Defense Procurement and Policy
*   **New Entry for Startups:** Former Secretary Wilbur Ross highlighted a significant policy shift within the DOD (led by officials like Secretary Hicks and Peter Feinberg) that welcomes innovative startups, a process that was previously too bureaucratic for new entrants.
*   **From Sophistication to Multiplication:** Historical defense policy prioritized high-tech sophistication; current threats, such as drone swarms, now require "multiplication"—the ability to produce massive quantities of units quickly.
*   **War of Attrition:** Malik emphasized that modern conflicts are won not just by the best technology, but by the speed at which a nation can replenish its arsenal.

## Reusable Space Technology and "The Gas Station on the Moon"
*   **Propulsion Innovation:** iRocket utilizes an "expander cycle" engine. By operating at lower temperatures and pressures, they increase the service life of critical components, enabling a launch vehicle to be refueled and redeployed within 24 hours.
*   **Patented Reusability:** The company has four patents pending, including a unique landing system and an upper-stage thermal shield for re-entry.
*   **Lunar Infrastructure:** Secretary Ross predicted a "Next Industrial Revolution" in space, including 3D printing, pharmaceutical manufacturing in zero-G, and using the moon as a refueling station (extracting hydrogen and oxygen from ice) for Mars missions.

## National Security and Intellectual Warfare
*   **Intellectual Espionage:** Ross warned that "intellectual warfare" is the new front of global competition. He highlighted the need for strict export controls on "dual-use" products—consumer tech that has military applications.
*   **Foreign Surveillance:** Ross expressed concern over foreign adversaries (specifically China) purchasing land near U.S. military bases for espionage purposes rather than agricultural or commercial value.
*   **Future Outlook:** iRocket confirmed plans to go public, with more specific details expected to be released within the next few months.

> "It’s highly unsustainable to fire a four million dollar Patriot missile at a twenty-five thousand dollar drone... It’s not the best missile system that wins the war, it’s how fast you can replenish the arsenal."
> — **Asad Malik**

> "Our defense system had been geared to winning by sophistication. Now you need sophistication but you need multiplication. You need very large numbers of units."
> — **Wilbur Ross**

> "The man on the moon is going to become a gas station attendant... to get to Mars most efficiently, you only want to load in enough fuel in the beginning to break the earth's gravitational pull and get to the moon."
> — **Wilbur Ross**
